newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Delta names acting CEO, chairman.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Delta names acting CEO, chairman.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. named two acting executives to head the company Thursday, buying more time to find a permanent replacement for retiring Chairman Ronald Allen at the nation's third largest carrier.
Delta said Maurice Worth has been named acting chief executive officer and Mary Johnston Evans, a member of Delta's board since 1983, will serve as acting non-executive chairman.

Worth, currently the airline's executive vice president of customer service, was named acting chief operating officer in May when Allen announced his retirement. Worth will oversee daily operations and Evans will handle board issues until a permanent chairman is named.
Allen's departure after 34 years with Delta surprised industry analysts, who suggested that his resignation followed a rift with the board about the company's strategic focus.

Analysts suspected Allen fell out of favour with the board after serveral small missteps, such as his attempted ouster of Chief Financial Officer Thomas Roeck. The board also cringed as Allen's sharp cost-cutting efforts began to take its toll on customer service and employee morale, analysts said.

To appease shareholders, employees and board members, the next head of Delta will have to be all things to all people, analysts said -- a "feel-good" leader, a visionary, and a bean counter. But having good chemistry with the board may be the most crucial prerequisite, they said.

Naming interim officers clears up some of the uncertainty for the airline in the midst of the peak summer travel season. But the lack of a clear candidate points to how difficult the choice is with competition stiff and fares under pressure.

"Walking into the Delta situation is not going to be easy. Most of the low-hanging fruit has already been picked. So getting Delta to the next level is going to be really tough," said Helane Becker, an airline analyst with Smith Barney.
Delta has been through a painful restructuring in recent years and has cleared many difficult hurdles, but is still trying to bolster its international service, analysts said.

"They cut maybe a little too much," said Jeff Long at J.P. Morgan. "They cut costs and now their costs are in pretty good shape. But ther reputation among passengers has slipped at a time when their competitors are really focusing on service, trying to attract business class passengers," said Long.
Business flyers are the most profitable customers for airlines.
The candidates for the top job at Delta include the usual suspects within the industry as well as some new faces.

The heirs apparent at AMR Corp.'s American Airlines and Continental Airlines Inc. are seen as top contenders, as is Hollis Harris, Delta's former president. But most analysts said Delta was unlikely to look to the past for its future leader.
Acting chief executive Worth, a 36-year veteran at Delta, said he was not a candidate for the job.
"I have not been interviewed for the job and I am doing the job that I have been assigned to do," Worth said -- taking the Atlanta-based carrier through a transition period.
"I'm concentrating my efforts on that," he said.
Once Delta names a permanent CEO, Worth said that he hopes to play "an active role at Delta."
The company declined to comment on how long its search would take or discuss potential candidates.
Analysts said Delta would move cautiously, given the recent boardroom scuffles at AT&T Corp. and other companies.
"Given what's happened with AT&T, they're going to be very mindful in making their selection. They don't want to rush into anything," Becker said.
At a news conference in Atlanta, Evans said Delta was not seeking dramatic change but would be open to having an executive that brings a fresh perspective to the industry.

Delta is looking for "someone who recognises the strengths that Delta has now and (can) help them to grow. Maybe someone who has a new look at the industry. We're looking inside and outside the industry," Evans said.
"We can always learn from outside, but I think we think the direction we're going is just right," she said.
